items.title: Your Smart Doorbell Is a Bigger Security Problem Than You Think — Here’s a Fix That Actually Scales
items.description:
What happens when you stop treating “lightweight crypto” and “blockchain” as two separate arguments, and start treating them as one system

There’s a decent chance that right now, somewhere in your house, there’s a $30 sensor quietly deciding whether to trust a stranger. Your smart doorbell. Your thermostat. Maybe a water leak detector under the sink you forgot existed. Each one is a tiny computer with a network connection, a battery it needs to survive on for years, and — usually — security that was clearly an afterthought.

That’s not a knock on the engineers who built them. It’s a genuinely hard problem. And it’s about to get a lot bigger: current projections put the number of connected edge devices at over twenty billion within the next few years. Every one of those is a potential entry point. The Mirai botnet, back in 2016, needed only a few hundred thousand hijacked cameras and routers to knock large parts of the internet offline. We’re not talking about a hundred thousand devices anymore. We’re talking about twenty billion.

So here’s the question this piece is about: how do you actually secure that many devices, when most of them don’t have the horsepower to run the security protocols we already trust?

The Straw-Sized Problem With Marathon-Sized Solutions

TLS 1.3 is a genuinely excellent protocol. OAuth 2.0 works great at web scale. If you’re reading this on a laptop or phone, both are protecting you right now without you noticing. The problem is that both were built for devices with room to spare — plenty of memory, plenty of CPU, and a power outlet nearby.

An edge sensor running off a coin-cell battery for three or four years doesn’t have that luxury. Asking it to do a full TLS handshake, carry around a kilobyte-plus certificate chain, and phone home to a centralized identity server every time it needs to prove who it is — that’s a bit like asking someone to run a marathon while breathing through a straw. Technically possible. Something’s going to give out before the finish line, though, and usually it’s the battery, or the latency, or (when engineers get impatient and start cutting corners) the actual security.

There’s a second problem hiding underneath the first one. Even a device that can afford a lightweight handshake still needs someone to vouch for it — some authority that says “yes, this device is allowed on the network.” Historically that’s a centralized identity provider. Which is convenient, until it isn’t: compromise that one server, and every device that trusted it inherits the compromise. Decentralized ledgers and smart contracts have been pitched as the fix here for years — automated, tamper-evident, no single point of failure. But blockchain has a well-earned reputation for being slow and heavy, and understandably, most IoT engineers have kept it at arm’s length.

What If These Are Actually the Same Problem?

Here’s the thing that surprised me going into this: almost nobody researches these two pieces together. There’s a whole body of work on lightweight ciphers — ASCON, compressed elliptic curve key exchange, that kind of thing — measured in isolation on a single chip. And there’s a whole separate body of work on blockchain-based device identity, usually tested on a few hundred simulated devices. Almost nobody asks what happens when you actually put both pieces in the same system and push it to the scale where it would matter — hundreds of thousands, or a million, concurrent devices.

So that’s what this project set out to do: build a two-layer framework, measure it properly, and see what breaks first.

Layer one handles device-to-gateway communication with ASCON — the cipher NIST just standardized specifically for constrained hardware — plus a compressed elliptic-curve key exchange (a Curve25519 variant). Both are dramatically cheaper, cycle-for-cycle, than the AES/RSA combo most systems default to.

Layer two handles the “should this device even be here?” question with a sharded, permissioned blockchain (Hyperledger Fabric) running smart contracts that make zero-trust access decisions — meaning every single request gets re-checked, not just the first one. The sharding matters a lot here: instead of routing every device’s authentication request through one global consensus process, the network is split into independent shards, each handling its own slice of devices. That’s the mechanism that keeps the ledger from becoming exactly the kind of single point of failure it was supposed to replace.

(Insert Figure: Authentication Latency CDF)

The Numbers — And the One That Actually Surprised Me

Compared against a conventional TLS 1.3 + centralized OAuth 2.0 setup, the hybrid framework cut median authentication latency by 66.6% — 46 milliseconds versus 138. It also cut the raw CPU-cycle cost of the cryptographic handshake by roughly 47%. Neither of those is shocking, exactly; that’s what you’d expect from swapping in lighter cryptography.

Here’s the part that actually surprised me. Going in, I assumed cryptography would be the bottleneck once you scaled the network up — that’s where almost all the existing lightweight-crypto literature focuses. It isn’t. Once the network passes somewhere around 40,000 concurrently authenticating devices, the bottleneck shifts almost entirely to the blockchain layer — specifically, to smart contract gas metering and endorsement coordination, not the cipher at all.

(Insert Figure: Smart Contract Execution Cost vs. Network Scale)

That’s not a subtle effect, either. Below that ~40,000-device threshold, execution cost per authentication stays essentially flat. Cross it, and cost starts climbing in an accelerating curve, not a straight line. And 40,000 devices isn’t some exotic hyperscale number — that’s a single mid-sized smart-city district, or a large industrial campus. Which means, practically speaking: if you’re building one of these systems, the dial you should be turning first is shard count and endorsement policy, not cipher choice. Most teams would probably spend their optimization budget in exactly the wrong place.

The Tail Is Where Systems Actually Fail

One more thing worth pulling out, because averages hide it: I compared the hybrid framework against two baselines — the TLS+OAuth setup mentioned above, and a “naively decentralized” alternative using conventional AES-256 paired with public Ethereum instead of a permissioned chain. On raw median latency, the Ethereum-backed baseline actually looked better than TLS+OAuth (124ms vs. 138ms).

But look at the 95th percentile instead of the median, and the story flips. The Ethereum-backed setup’s tail stretches out to 256ms — nearly five times its own median — because public-chain consensus delay is wildly variable. The hybrid framework’s 95th percentile, by contrast, stays close to its median (51ms vs. 46ms). In other words: it’s not just faster, it’s predictable, and predictability is usually what actually matters for anything approaching real-time control.

(Insert Figure: Edge Device Battery Drain Over Time)

Battery life follows the same pattern you’d hope for: over a simulated 30-day deployment, a device running the hybrid framework still has over 80% of its battery left. The TLS+OAuth device has burned through more than 40%. Small per-handshake savings don’t look like much on their own, but multiply them by a few hundred authentication events a day, every day, for years, and they compound into something that actually changes how often someone has to physically go swap a battery.

Where This Is Genuinely Useful — And Where It Isn’t

Sharding by district or zone maps naturally onto how smart-city networks are already organized administratively, so this isn’t a purely theoretical fit — a city doesn’t need every traffic sensor authenticating against one global consensus process, and splitting by geography or department is a fairly natural boundary to shard along.

I want to be upfront about where this framework doesn’t help, though. It doesn’t protect against someone physically stealing a device and extracting its key material — that needs hardware-level protection (secure elements, physically unclonable functions), which is a different problem entirely. And a small permissioned shard is still theoretically vulnerable to collusion among its own endorsing peers if that peer set is small and not independently governed — sharding contains the blast radius of that risk, but doesn’t eliminate it.

(Insert Figure: Cryptographic Handshake Overhead)

One more honest note, because it changed how I think about where the real savings come from: the popular assumption is that lightweight ciphers save you money on bulk encryption. They don’t, really — signature verification is the single most expensive stage in both the lightweight and conventional setups. The actual savings show up in key generation and exchange, where the compressed elliptic-curve approach cuts cycle counts by more than half compared to RSA-2048. If you’re optimizing a system like this, that’s the stage that deserves the attention, not the cipher doing the bulk encryption.

The Takeaway

Twenty billion devices are coming whether the security infrastructure is ready or not. The good news, based on what this framework shows, is that lightweight cryptography and decentralized trust aren’t competing approaches you have to choose between — they’re complementary, and combining them well outperforms either one alone, plus the conventional centralized approach most systems still default to.

The less obvious but arguably more useful finding is where the real ceiling sits: not in the cipher, but in how the ledger itself is sharded and configured. That’s a fixable, tunable problem — which is a much better place to be than “we need a fundamentally faster cryptographic primitive.”

items.title: India Generates Enough Electricity. The Problem Is Everything That Happens Next.
items.description:
Where does our power disappear — and how can autonomous AI systems finally fix the last mile?

From plant to home: thermal towers, wind turbines, rooftop solar and a smart meter on the long journey of one unit of electricity.
Imagine a May afternoon in Nagpur. The sun is blazing, your AC is working overtime, and somewhere far away a solar park is producing more power than it has all year. And yet, in that same moment, a chunk of that solar power is being thrown away, while a chunk of the power that reaches your street vanishes on the way — as heat in old wires, as leaks in ageing transformers, and as theft through illegal taps.
This is the strange paradox of Indian power today: we are generating enough, but we are still losing too much. In this article, we’ll first look at real data from official and reputed sources, then discuss what it actually means, identify the research gaps, and finally propose a practical ML/AI autonomous methodology that can genuinely optimise Indian power distribution.
No jargon walls. Simple words. Let’s go.
Part 1 — The Data: What the Numbers Say
1. Generation: We’re producing more than ever
India’s installed capacity reached about 476 GW by June 2025, and peak power shortages fell from 4.2% (2013–14) to just 0.1% (2024–25).
Solar has crossed ~117 GW and wind ~51.7 GW.
Demand is not slowing down. The IEA expects Indian electricity demand to grow at roughly 6.4% per year through 2030.
Meanwhile, thermal plants — still our backbone — face falling capacity utilisation as renewables grow.
So the generation story is mostly healthy. The stress lives after the plant gate.
2. Distribution: The leaky middle
India’s AT&C losses (Aggregate Technical & Commercial losses — a fancy term for “power that left the substation but never got paid for”) fell from 22.62% in FY 2013–14 to 15.04% in FY 2024–25.
DISCOMs (our distribution companies) finally recorded a positive profit of ₹2,701 crore in FY 2024–25, after a loss of ₹25,553 crore the previous year.
The cost-recovery gap (ACS–ARR) narrowed from ₹0.78/kWh to ₹0.06/kWh.
Good news, sincerely. But look closer:
On the World Bank’s T&D loss indicator, India still sits far above the ~8% global norm seen in well-run systems. Historically, state-wise AT&C losses have ranged anywhere from 18% to over 60% in the worst utilities.
The World Bank notes DISCOMs’ combined annual losses at ₹67,800 crore (~$8.1 billion), with cumulative debt around $83.5 billion.
A big slice of commercial loss is plain theft and billing leakage — a problem that has historically cost India tens of thousands of crores, and one that globally accounts for ~$89.3 billion in losses for utilities.
3. Unutilised power: The energy we throw away
Here’s the newest wound — renewable curtailment, i.e., switching off solar and wind even when they could generate, because the grid can’t absorb it safely. Solar and wind are “use-it-or-lose-it” sources.
India lost 2.3 TWh of solar generation in the second half of 2025 due to grid-security constraints.
In Q1 2026, about 470 GWh of renewables were curtailed, of which 300 GWh was directly due to transmission constraints.
In Q2 2026 alone, India curtailed 8.13 TWh of solar to keep the grid secure.
That’s billions of units of zero-fuel, zero-carbon energy — evaporated.
4. The fix in progress: Smart meters (RDSS)
The Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS) targets 25 crore prepaid smart meters. As on 31 December 2025, 3.90 crore smart meters were installed under the scheme. That’s real progress — and, honestly, also a reminder that the visibility problem is still ~85% unsolved.
Data Sources
Central Electricity Authority (CEA) Dashboard — https://cea.nic.in/dashboard/
National Power Portal (Govt. of India) — https://npp.gov.in/
PIB — DISCOM performance & AT&C losses — https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2215761
PIB — Smart meter progress under RDSS — https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2222217
RDSS Official Portal, Ministry of Power — https://rdss.powermin.gov.in/rdss
World Bank — T&D losses (% of output), India — https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/EG.ELC.LOSS.ZS?locations=IN
World Bank — India distribution modernization results — https://www.worldbank.org/en/results/2025/07/10/reinvigorating-india-s-electricity-distribution-for-access-reliability-and-digitalization
IEA — India country page & Electricity 2026 — https://www.iea.org/countries/india
Ember Energy — India curtailment analyses — https://ember-energy.org/latest-updates/india-lost-2-3-twh-of-solar-generation-due-to-grid-security-concerns-largely-concentrated-in-the-second-half-of-2025/ and https://ember-energy.org/latest-updates/india-lost-300-million-units-of-renewable-energy-owing-to-transmission-constraints-in-q1-2026/
Mercom India — Q2 2026 solar curtailment — https://www.mercomindia.com/india-curtailed-8-13-twh-solar-power-in-q2-2026-to-maintain-grid-security
Prayas (Energy Group) — smart metering ground reality — https://energy.prayaspune.org/power-perspectives/smart-metering-in-india-a-work-in-progress
NITI Aayog (ICED) — energy mix overview — https://iced.niti.gov.in/energy/

The leaky pipe: energy enters from a plant, drips out through cracks (technical dissipation + theft), until a modern sensor-fitted section finally doesn’t leak.
Part 2 — Discussion: Reading Between the Numbers
Here’s the honest picture. India has successfully fixed the quantity problem (enough capacity, near-zero shortage) but not the quality-of-journey problem. Every unit of electricity travels through a chain — substation → feeder → transformer → meter — and at each hop, two kinds of leaks occur:
Technical losses (dissipation): energy lost as heat in overloaded conductors, old transformers and poor voltage control. This is physics, and it’s manageable.
Commercial losses: theft, unbilled energy, faulty meters, delayed billing. This is human, and it’s stubborn.
The improvement from 22.6% to 15% AT&C is real, but it’s uneven — a handful of good utilities (mostly private or reformed ones) are pulling the average up, while many state DISCOMs still bleed. And now a third leak has appeared: curtailment. We built solar faster than we built the network’s ability to absorb it.
The cruel irony? The same missing ingredient causes all three leaks: blindness. Most feeders in India are still invisible in real time. You cannot fix what you cannot see at 15-minute granularity. This is exactly why the smart-meter drive matters — and exactly why data alone is not enough. Meters produce data; decisions must come from intelligence layered on top.
Part 3 — The Research Gaps
Academia has not been idle. Reviews now cover 150+ studies on ML in power systems, ML has been applied to load forecasting, fault detection and distribution optimisation, and ML-based non-technical loss (theft) detection is an active area. Reinforcement learning (RL) — the “learning by trial and reward” branch of AI — is considered the most promising tool for distribution management, with new benchmarks like RL2Grid appearing.
But when you look for solutions that would actually work in an Indian DISCOM, the gaps are glaring:
Simulation-to-field gap: Most papers test on foreign benchmark networks (like the IEEE 33-bus system), not on real Indian feeder data with single-phase supplies, unmetered agricultural loads and messy GIS maps.
Point solutions, no closed loop: Studies do forecasting or theft detection or voltage control — in isolation. Nobody ships an integrated system that measures, decides, acts and verifies.
Theft models don’t travel: A model trained in one state fails in another; labelled theft data is scarce, and papers rarely co-design the field workflow (work order → raid → verification) that makes detection money-saving.
RL stays on paper: Safety, physical constraints and model drift in real weak-grid conditions are under-researched; robust approaches (like RL combined with distributionally robust optimisation) are brand new.
Dirty-data reality: With only ~3.9 of 25 crore smart meters installed, models must survive missing and corrupted data — a topic almost untouched in literature.
Curtailment is studied at transmission level, while distribution-level flexibility (rooftop solar, batteries, EVs, shiftable loads) to soak up unutilised power is barely explored for India.
No trust layer: Explainability, regulator confidence, and fairness between urban and rural feeders are missing; there’s no “autonomy levels” framework (like self-driving cars have) for grid AI.

Left: the overloaded, sparking, tangled legacy feeder. Right: the same feeder after optimisation — neat green flows, sensors, storage and a tiny AI controller.
Part 4 — Proposed Methodology: “Feeder-Brain”, an Autonomous ML/AI System
Here’s a methodology designed to close those gaps — not another dashboard, but a closed-loop autonomous system that lives at the feeder level and rides on top of the RDSS smart-meter investment.
Layer 1 — Sense (cheap, incremental)
Ingest 15-minute smart-meter reads, substation SCADA data, and low-cost IoT sensors on distribution transformers (load, voltage, temperature). No big-bang hardware; start where meters exist.
Layer 2 — See: a Digital Twin + real loss accounting
Build a simple digital twin (a software copy) of each feeder. Every 15 minutes, do transformer-level energy accounting: energy in − energy billed = loss. A hybrid physics+ML model splits it into technical vs commercial loss, so the utility finally knows where loss happens, not just the national average.
Layer 3 — Predict
Ensemble forecasting (gradient-boosted trees + LSTM/Transformer) for feeder load and rooftop solar, weather-driven, from 15 minutes to 24 hours ahead. This is the input every other layer trusts.
Layer 4 — Detect
Theft and fault detection using graph-based ML on consumption patterns (sudden drops, night-load anomalies, meter-bypass signatures). Crucially, every alert ships with a plain-language explanation and auto-generates a work order — closing the detection-to-revenue loop that pure research misses.
Layer 5 — Act: the autonomous brain
A multi-agent deep reinforcement learning controller (in the spirit of RL2Grid and safe RL–DRO frameworks) that continuously performs:
Network reconfiguration (shifting load between feeders via tie-switches),
Volt/VAR control (tap changers, capacitor banks) to cut technical dissipation,
Storage & flexible-load dispatch to absorb midday solar and cut curtailment,
Set-points for rooftop solar inverters as a last resort, fairly rotated.
Two safety rules make it deployable: (a) every action is first tested inside the digital twin against hard physics limits; (b) a small edge controller at the substation keeps basic protection running even when internet connectivity dies — cloud trains, edge acts.
Layer 6 — Govern: autonomy levels + explainability
Borrow the self-driving car idea: Level 1 (AI advises) → Level 2 (AI acts, human approves) → Level 3 (AI acts autonomously within pre-approved limits) → Level 4 (full autonomy on routine actions only). Engineers see an explainable dashboard; regulators see audit trails. This is the trust layer every past project skipped.

The Feeder-Brain: an AI chip at the substation, autonomously balancing solar, batteries, streetlights and homes through glowing live connections.
Proof it works: the pilot design
Run 50 pilot feeders across 3 states (high-loss, low-loss, solar-rich) against 50 matched control feeders for 12 months. Success metrics: AT&C < 10% on pilot feeders, 20–40% fewer outage minutes (SAIDI/SAIFI), ≥30% less curtailment on solar-rich feeders, and rupee value of loss recovered. If the money shows up in the DISCOM’s ACS–ARR gap, scale it — that’s the optimisation that actually matters.
Closing Thought
India’s power story has moved from “will the lights turn on?” to “how much of what we make actually reaches the person who pays for it?” The data says we’ve come far — 15% AT&C, profitable DISCOMs, 476 GW of capacity. The data also says the last mile is still leaking money, and now leaking clean energy too.
The tools to fix this — smart meters, ML, reinforcement learning, edge computing — already exist. What we need is a methodology that treats the feeder as the patient, the data as the pulse, and the AI as a supervised, explainable, autonomous doctor.
The grid of the future won’t just be strong. It will be awake.

References & Further Reading (research)

View the updated Workbook

ML for non-technical loss detection — Nature Scientific Reports: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-20048-z
Optimised power distribution using ML — Kumar, 2024: https://ijrasht.com/index.php/files/article/download/125/63
AI/ML for distributed energy systems review — Satpathy, 2026: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261925018392
ML & AI techniques in power systems (150+ studies review) — Energy Science & Engineering: https://scijournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ese3.70449
RL-based intelligent control for distribution management — Al-Saadi, 2023: https://www.mdpi.com/1996-1073/16/4/1608
RL2Grid: benchmarking RL in power grids — arXiv: https://arxiv.org/html/2503.23101v1
Safe RL + robust optimisation for resilient dispatch — Nature Scientific Reports, 2026: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-50532-z
RL in power systems overview — Bernadić, 2023: https://sciendo.com/pdf/10.2478/bhee-2023-0004

items.title: Decoding Shark Tank India: What the Data Actually Tells Us About Startup Success
items.description:
Forget the reality TV drama. We looked at the hard numbers behind investor confidence, consumer demand, and sectoral performance (2021–2025).

Based on research by Abhishek Mondal

📺 Beyond the Bidding Wars

We all love the dramatic “Namaste” moments and the intense bidding wars on Shark Tank India. But what happens when the cameras stop rolling? Which businesses actually survive, and which ones just made for good TV?

Thanks to a recent aggregated multi-seasonal analysis (spanning 2021–2025), we finally have a clear, data-backed look at India’s startup ecosystem. By analyzing sectoral performance across 7 major industries, the research tracks how investor confidence, consumer demand, and sales performanceinteract.

Here is the short, crisp breakdown of the data.

📊 The 4 Pillars of Startup Survival

The research evaluated every sector across four critical metrics. Here is what the numbers reveal:

1. Yearly Revenue (The Scalability Test)

Total revenue generated across tracked sectors: ₹670.43 Lakhs.

  • 🏆 The Leader: Business Services dominates with ₹216.99 Lakhs (nearly a third of the entire pie!), proving the massive demand for consulting, IT solutions, and B2B outsourcing.
  • 📈 The Strong Runners-Up: Lifestyle/Home (₹151.82L), Manufacturing (₹143.98L), and Fitness/Sports (₹143.56L) form a solid second tier.
  • 📉 The Laggards: Hardware recorded exactly ₹0, while Entertainment scraped by at a mere ₹0.65 Lakhs.

2. Monthly Sales (The Consumer Stickiness Metric)

Yearly revenue shows scale, but monthly sales prove consumer demand and product stickiness. Total monthly sales: ₹54.89 Lakhs.

  • 🏠 The Shift in Spending: Lifestyle/Home takes the crown here with ₹25.24 Lakhs, showing that Indian consumers are heavily investing in comfort and home upgrades.
  • 🧘 Health is Wealth: Fitness/Sports trails nicely at ₹11.06 Lakhs, riding the massive post-pandemic wellness wave.
  • 🏭 Industrial Balance: Manufacturing (₹9.83L) and Business Services (₹7.07L) maintain a healthy balance between B2C and B2B needs.

3. Received Offers (The “Hype” & Investor Interest)

Sharks made a total of 98 offers across the board.

  • 🛠️ Make in India: Manufacturing led the pack with 31 offers, showing high investor confidence in production-driven enterprises.
  • 🛍️ Consumer Favorites: Lifestyle/Home (23 offers) and Business Services (22 offers) followed closely.
  • ⚠️ Red Flags: Entertainment and Hardware received just 1 offer each, signaling extremely low investor appetite.

4. Accepted Offers (The Deal Reality)

Out of 98 offers, a massive 81 were accepted (an 82%+ conversion rate!).

  • 🤝 The Closers: Manufacturing sealed the deal 26 times, cementing its dominance in successful negotiations. Business Services (18) and Lifestyle/Home (17) followed.
  • 🚪 The Disconnect: Weak industries failed to progress. Hardware and Entertainment barely moved the needle despite minimal offers.

🗂️ The Ecosystem Verdict: Who Made the Cut?

Based on the intersection of revenue, sales, and deal conversions, the research categorizes the startup landscape into three distinct buckets:

  • 🟢 Strong Performers (The Pillars): Business Services, Manufacturing, and Lifestyle/Home. These sectors benefit from India’s push toward self-reliance and shifting consumer behaviors.
  • 🟡 Average Performers (The Steady Climbers): Fitness/Sports/Outdoors and Liquor/Alcohol. They show promise, resilience, and a loyal customer base, but lack the explosive scalability Sharks usually hunt for.
  • 🔴 Weak Performers (The Struggling Giants): Entertainment and Hardware. Despite being massive markets globally, they face structural barriers and poor execution in the Indian context.

💡 The Big Takeaway

The biggest lesson from this data?

While a D2C lifestyle brand or a solid B2B service might easily secure funding and scale revenue, capital-heavy or niche sectors like Hardware are being left in the dust. For founders, the roadmap is clear: build for real consumer stickiness, and the Sharks will follow.

📚 Source & Further Reading:

  • Original Research: Industry Insights from Shark Tank India: A Sector-wise Research Analysis by Abhishek Mondal (Lovely Professional University).
  • Dataset & Paper Link: Access the full research data on Zenodo here
